rule: A quarter-on-quarter change of exactly a thousand times is a change of unit, not of the portfolio, and is removed before anything is measured
example: Every manager's disclosed book appears to grow a thousandfold at the end of 2022, when the reporting unit changed from thousands of dollars to dollars (68 of the 92 cases). The other 24 are single filings where one manager used the wrong unit. Lone Pine filed the quarter ending 2014-12-31 with a book a thousand times the quarter before it and the quarter after it, and neither neighbour is wrong.

issue: Share counts are on an old basis after a split
rule: A persistent jump matching a known split ratio is taken out of the whole earlier history, so share counts and prices are on the same basis
example: NVIDIA reported 548 million shares in 2009; against prices that carry two later splits the same company has 21.9 billion on today's basis, a factor of 40. Without this the company sits in the smallest size group for years, and every size and value measure built on it is wrong.

issue: One-off errors in reported share counts
rule: A filing five times its neighbours in both directions, in a run of at most three, is dropped rather than believed
example: A company files its share count in thousands one quarter and in units the next, so it looks as though it was taken over and then un-taken over. 1,133 of 52,007 filed share counts are dropped this way.

issue: Securities that never reach a price
rule: A position that cannot be matched to a priced security is left out of every portfolio, and the share left out is reported for every quarter
example: Most are companies that were bought or renamed, so no price history exists to buy. 22 identifiers that the reference tables get wrong are corrected by hand, mostly foreign listings and share classes.

issue: Impossible monthly returns in the price history
rule: A gain of more than 300% in a month from a price under $5 is treated as a bad price and left blank rather than earned
example: These are almost all delisted or near-bankrupt shells whose quoted price bounces between cents. Left in, a handful of them would carry a whole portfolio's return.
